p1: November 1954.
A fighter is hanging in the sky.
Nose pointed straight up.
Propellers roaring.
And it's coming down…
tail first.
The pilot can't see the ground ahead of him.
It's behind him.
So he twists round in his seat, looks back over his shoulder, and lowers more than five tonnes of fighter toward the earth, mostly by eye.
Come down too fast, and it slams onto its tail.
Drift, and it can tip over.
His rival at Lockheed built a plane to do exactly this.
It never once managed it.
This one did.
This is the Convair XFY-1 Pogo.
So why would anyone build a fighter you have to land backwards?
And if it actually worked, why has almost nobody heard of it?
The answer comes down to one problem.
And by the end of this video, you'll see exactly why it helped kill the Pogo.
It starts at sea.
During the Second World War, Allied convoys crossing the Atlantic faced attacks from German U-boats and aircraft.
Protecting those ships meant getting fighters over the ocean—but conventional fighters needed runways or aircraft carriers, and carriers were expensive and limited in number.
After the war, the Navy asked a radical question.
What if any ship could carry its own fighter?
No runway.
No catapult.
No carrier.
Just a small platform on the deck.
After years of study, the Navy wanted a fighter that could take off straight up from a ship and land straight back down on it.
In 1951, it ordered prototypes from Convair and Lockheed.
And both companies came up with the same basic idea.
A fighter that sits on its tail.
And here's the catch nobody could design away.
If a plane takes off pointing at the sky, it has to land pointing at the sky.
The pilot sits in the nose, at the very top.
So when he comes down to land, the ground is behind his back.
Keep that in mind.
It's the whole story.
Convair's answer looked like nothing else in the sky.
A short, fat fuselage.
A delta wing.
And a huge tail fin above and below, so from behind it looked like a cross.
It had no conventional landing gear.
Just four small wheels, on the tips of the wings and the fins.
When it was parked, it didn't sit.
It stood.
In the nose was an Allison T40, really two turbine engines driving one gearbox, about 5,850 horsepower.
It turned two propellers, each with three blades, sixteen feet across, about five metres, spinning in opposite directions.
Here's how it hung in the air.
To hover, the propellers have to push upward harder than the whole aircraft weighs.
At maximum takeoff weight, about sixteen thousand pounds, that's over seven tonnes.
More thrust than weight, it climbs.
Less, and it sinks.
The throttle controls the climb and the sink.
But the pilot still has to balance it on its tail with the controls, every second.
And there's a second problem.
Spin one huge propeller one way, and the airframe wants to spin the other way.
That's Newton's third law.
So the Pogo has two.
One turns clockwise, one turns anticlockwise, and their twist cancels out.
Without that, it would just spin on its tail like a top.
p2: Getting it into the air turned out to be the easy part.
Getting it back down is where this story gets frightening.
In the spring of 1954, the Pogo was taken to Moffett Field in California, inside Hangar One, a building so big it was built to house a Navy airship.
For safety, it flew tied to cables, hovering under the roof.
Over and over, it rose, hung there, and came back down.
The man flying it was Convair's test pilot, James "Skeets" Coleman.
Just getting in was strange.
He climbed a ladder to a cockpit two storeys up, and settled in almost flat on his back, looking straight at the ceiling.
For vertical flight, his seat tilted about 45 degrees toward the instrument panel, but landing still left him struggling to see the ground.
On the first of August, 1954, the cables came off.
The Pogo took off outside, free, for the first time.
Taking off was simple.
Point it up, open the throttle, and climb.
Once it was high enough, the pilot pushed the nose over, and it flew like a normal plane.
Landing was the problem.
He had to slow down, pull the nose up until the whole aircraft was pointing at the sky, and hang there on the propellers.
Then he had to come down tail-first.
Now look at what he could actually see.
In front of him, sky.
Below him, his own aircraft.
The only way to see the ground was to twist round and look back over his shoulder.
From there, he had to judge three things at once.
How high am I?
How fast am I sinking?
And am I drifting sideways?
A radar altimeter in the wingtip drove three warning lights to help Coleman judge his descent.
But the lights couldn't do the landing for him.
Come down too fast, and the impact could damage the aircraft or make it tip over.
Drift sideways, and the narrow landing stance left little room for error.
And all the time, any gust of wind is pushing on that big wing and those tall fins.
He's doing this backwards, mostly by eye, in a fighter that weighs as much as four cars.
On the second of November, 1954, Coleman did the whole thing.
Straight up from the ground, over into level flight, back up to vertical, and down, backwards, onto its tail.
No aircraft like it had ever done that before.
It earned him the Harmon Trophy, one of aviation's highest awards.
The Pogo worked.
But it took a pilot of Coleman's skill to land it.
